source.title: On the creation of narrow AI: hierarchy and nonlocality of neural network skills
source.authors: Eric J. Michaud; Asher Parker-Sartori; Max Tegmark

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It conceptually tests whether skills are localized to prunable neurons or other components, using ablation scores and pruning outcomes rather than measuring neurons' responses to different inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses polysemanticity and distributed representations, but does not measure neuron activation responses to unrelated inputs or count polysemantic neurons. Its own results concern whether task skills are localized to components; these are recorded as findings that fit none of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper names polysemanticity and superposition only as background for its own question: whether task skills sit in separate prunable neurons. It never measures how neurons respond to unrelated inputs, counts polysemantic neurons, or tests a cause. Its closest result (R1) shows some neurons matter to several CMSP subtasks, judged by ablation loss change. That is task-importance overlap, a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version. The reader's 'tests'/T2 contradicts its own note that every version is untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors also conclude that narrow skills can require broad training data when skills are hierarchical (the CMSP curriculum effect). They also find that pruning plus recovery outperforms distillation and training from scratch on MNIST and Python LLMs. In LLMs, random pruning performs similarly to attribution pruning, and all pruning methods unlearn non-Python skills with roughly similar effectiveness, except attribution pruning at 30% sparsity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies task-component localization through ablation scoring and pruning, rather than the original sources' neuron-response visualizations or activation-function comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: CMSP skill entanglement varies with seed and width. Group-lasso regularization changes pruning and unlearning outcomes. In the LLM recovery comparison, attribution pruning is initially better than random pruning, but the reported gap is eventually recovered.

fits_no_version.finding: In unregularized CMSP MLPs, some neurons have high ablation scores across most subtasks, including subtasks from separate skill trees.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual neurons can be causally important to several distinct task skills, so skills are not localized to disjoint neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning for subtask {0,1,2} often leaves {3,4,5} recoverable, but the degree of entanglement varies strongly by seed and width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How well task skills localize to neurons varies across training runs of the same architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Group-lasso training on the target task made CMSP networks more prunable, and {3,4,5} was not recoverable at any sparsity level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Group-sparsity regularization can align task skills with prunable components.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-3.2-1B on Python, random pruning plus recovery reaches nearly the same loss as attribution pruning (1.301 vs about 1.3 nats).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-relevant features in LLMs are not localized to a set of 'Python' neurons that attribution can identify.

record.problems: The paper itself notes that CMSP is a contrived toy task and that the relevance of its dynamics to natural tasks is unclear. The CMSP pruning results vary by seed and width. The LLM experiments use a simple attribution-pruning approach, and the authors say they did not optimally scale hyperparameters. Several pruning curves are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's benchmark-specific unlearning accuracies and the broader MNIST and LLM efficiency comparisons are not included: they report downstream pruning or specialization performance, not neuron responses or component overlap relevant to the claim.

untested.parts: No image-classifier neurons or their input responses are examined.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in Llama-3.2-1B, and no layer distribution, is measured.
Superposition is cited as a proposed explanation only; capacity pressure is not varied.
Incidental origins (initialization, regularization, training noise) are cited but not tested.
Group lasso changes prunability, but the share of polysemantic neurons is not measured across architectures or regularizers.
No improved explanation tools are applied to neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemanticity appears only in Section 3.3 background and in the conclusion's framing. This is not one of the original sources. No verdicts are given because no row measures what any version names.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neurons or responses to image inputs are measured.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models, or their responses to unrelated tokens or contexts, is measured.
The paper describes superposition as a proposed explanation, but does not test whether capacity pressure causes the observed nonlocality.
The paper does not test whether polysemanticity arises from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.

Group-lasso training affects pruning and unlearning in these experiments, but the paper does not measure how activation functions, architectures, or regularization change the share of polysemantic neurons.
The paper does not use improved feature explanations to establish that mixed neuron responses share one coherent feature.
The paper does not compare neuron polysemanticity under different activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: 2-hidden-layer MLPs trained on CMSP
rows.operation_detail: Compared neuron ablation scores across CMSP subtasks.
rows.measure: Absolute change in loss when ablating each neuron, across subtasks
rows.note: The authors state that some neurons have high ablation scores across multiple subtasks, including subtasks in different skill trees. No individual score values are stated.
rows.check: Ablation-score overlap across subtasks measures shared importance to tasks, not responses to unrelated inputs, so it is not polysemanticity as V1/V2 define it. Values are figure only.

rows.subject: 2-hidden-layer MLPs trained on CMSP
rows.size_stated: widths 64, 128, 256, 512, and 1024 are shown in Appendix Figure 10
rows.operation_detail: Greedily pruned neurons by ablation score on subtask {0,1,2}; evaluated performance on {0,1,2} and {3,4,5}, including after 1,000 recovery steps.
rows.measure: Whether pruning that retains recoverable performance on {0,1,2} also removes performance on {3,4,5}
rows.note: The authors report that the two skill trees are often entangled and that some performance on {3,4,5} can still be recovered, but that the degree of entanglement varies by seed and width; some networks robustly unlearn the other skill.
rows.check: This is a pruning or unlearning outcome for the study's own method, not a measure of neuron polysemanticity. The 'partial' state reflects seed- and width-dependent entanglement relative to no version.

rows.subject: 2-hidden-layer MLPs trained on CMSP
rows.stage_stated: additional training on subtask {0,1,2}, then pruning
rows.operation_detail: Applied group-lasso regularization while training on {0,1,2}, then recomputed neuron ablation scores and pruned.
rows.measure: Prunability while retaining {0,1,2}, and recoverability of {3,4,5}
rows.value: The authors report more aggressive pruning while retaining {0,1,2}; performance on {3,4,5} could not be recovered at any sparsity level.
rows.note: This is a result about making task skills more separable for pruning, not a measurement of neuron response polysemanticity.
rows.check: This is the study's own group-lasso method against unregularized pruning. It measures prunability and unlearning, not the share of polysemantic neurons, so it cannot speak to V5.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B
rows.stage_stated: pretrained model; recovery training on Python documents
rows.operation_detail: Pruned neurons and residual-stream dimensions using attribution scores or random selection, then recovery-trained on Python documents.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss on Python documents after recovery
rows.value: At step 5365, the randomly pruned model had loss 1.301 nats, described as almost identical to the attribution-pruned model that first matched the original model's performance.
rows.note: The authors say attribution pruning is initially better than random pruning, but that the gap is eventually recovered. This tests task-component localization only indirectly.
rows.check: This compares the study's own pruning methods (attribution vs random) on recovered loss. It is a method comparison, not a measure of neuron polysemanticity, and should not be scored against any version.
